title: 2022 Report on the State of the Legal Market: A Challenging Road to Recovery
pub: Thomson Reuters Institute and Georgetown Law Center on Ethics and the Legal Profession
author: Thomson Reuters Institute · Georgetown Law Center on Ethics and the Legal Profession

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report does not assess AI’s jagged task-level capabilities, verification needs or selective deployment. Instead, it redirects work redesign toward post-pandemic talent retention, hybrid-work equity and broad operational flexibility, treating AI-assisted processes as one component of a wider organisational transition.

st.t: Firm profitability: Revenue growth can hide cost fragility
st.an: The report directly supports the proposition that strong profits may conceal cost fragility. It records continued profit growth in 2021 while showing that rapidly rising associate compensation, exceptional turnover and limited productivity improvement threatened future profitability. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution about baselines by noting that comparisons with volatile 2020 could overstate the recovery.
qs: As can be  seen, all segments of the market seem well positioned for continued profit growth in 2021.
And it’s a change that will surely impact law firm  profitability in the coming year.

st.t: Firm resilience: High profits may conceal structural weakness
st.an: The report supports the core proposition that strong financial performance is not dispositive of resilience. It contrasts firms’ financial survival with a materially changed operating environment and identifies talent competition, record turnover, hybrid work and operational flexibility as continuing vulnerabilities. It does not address the cluster’s AI, buyer-power or pricing mechanisms, so its support is narrower and grounded mainly in workforce and post-pandemic adaptation pressures.
qs: Notwithstanding the fact that most firms have survived the pandemic quite well from a  financial standpoint, the new work environment that is emerging in the post-COVID era  will be distinctly different from anything that firms have encountered before.

These issues include:  (i) responding to the fierce competition for legal and other professional talent; (ii) facing the  crisis of retaining the talent firms already have; (iii) successfully navigating the hybrid work  model; and (iv) remaining operationally flexible in responding to further changes that may  emerge in the market.

kp.k: Technology acceptance increased; AI investment is recommended
kp.d: The report identifies broader acceptance of technology in legal service delivery as a pandemic effect and reports technology spending growth of 7.1% in the 12 months through November 2021. It recommends investment in AI-assisted work processes alongside digital communications, but presents no measured AI-specific effects on employment, productivity or legal outcomes.
qs: Third, the pandemic has broadened the acceptance of the role of technology in the effective delivery of legal services.
making appropriate investments in technology to keep the firm on the cutting edge of  digital communications and artificial intelligence-assisted work processes;

kp.k: Financial recovery requires careful baseline comparisons
kp.d: Financial evidence comes from 171 U.S.-based firms: 51 Am Law 100, 55 Am Law Second Hundred and 65 Midsize firms outside the Am Law 200. Demand through November 2021 grew 4.0% against 2020 but only 1.0% against 2019. The report cautions that pandemic disruption, followed by recovery, rate increases and expense reductions, makes 2020 an anomalous comparison year.
qs: This data is based on reported results from 171 U.S.-based law firms,  including 51 Am Law 100 firms, 55 Am Law Second Hundred firms, and 65 additional Midsize firms (outside of the Am Law 200).
demand posted its two strongest quarterly growth rates in the last decade, ending up 4.0%  (on a YTD basis) compared to 2020, although only up 1.0% compared to 2019.

kp.k: Transactional practices drove recovery above pre-pandemic demand
kp.d: Corporate work, including M&A, and real estate drove demand recovery. Through November 2021, corporate demand was 8.1% above 2020 and 6.9% above 2019; real estate was 10.0% above 2020 and 4.8% above 2019. Only corporate and real estate practices showed positive growth against 2019, offsetting weaker recoveries in litigation, labor and employment, and intellectual property.
qs: Demand growth, as shown below in Figure 3, was driven primarily by real estate and  corporate (including M&A) practice areas
with only the corporate (including M&A) and real estate  practices showing positive growth.

kp.k: Rates and collections strengthened despite changing timekeeper mix
kp.d: Worked rates—negotiated client rates—rose 3.9% across firms through November 2021, including 5.6% at Am Law 100 firms, 3.4% at Am Law Second Hundred firms and 3.0% at Midsize firms. The report suggests concentrated corporate demand enabled larger firms to select work more carefully. Other professional fee earners, including paralegals and project managers, experienced faster demand growth than lawyers from Q2 2021, moderating average worked-rate growth. Collection realization against worked rates reached 90.6%, its highest level since 2009.
qs: through November 2021, worked rates for all timekeepers4  across all firms grew 3.9% on a YTD basis
starting in Q2 2021, other professional fee earners have experienced growth rates much  higher than lawyers.
the average collection realization against worked rates across the market was 90.6%, the  highest level seen since 2009.

kp.k: Hiring moderated productivity gains during demand recovery
kp.d: The report attributes accelerated hiring partly to firms bringing in both the 2021 associate class and the class deferred from 2020. Headcount growth reached 3.9% by late November, while average daily demand per lawyer through November was only 0.3% above 2019. Average monthly billable hours were 124 in 2021 versus 134 in 2007. Applying the 2021 average worked rate of $533, the report calculates a hypothetical revenue difference of $63,960 per lawyer annually; this is an hours-based comparison, not evidence of AI-driven productivity.
qs: many firms  brought in two new classes of associates (the 2021 class and the class that was deferred from  2020).
productivity improved as compared to 2020, but was only 0.3% above the  average daily demand per lawyer in 2019.
the decline in billable hours since 2007 would represent a current cost to the average law firm of  $5,330 per lawyer per month, or $63,960 per lawyer per year.

kp.k: Rising compensation increased costs despite strong profitability
kp.d: On a rolling 12-month basis through November 2021, direct expenses rose 8.8% and overhead 5.1%. Associate compensation per FTE rose 11.3% overall and 15.6% at Am Law 100 firms. Nevertheless, the report expected firms to finish 2021 in good financial shape: Am Law firms continued double-digit profit-per-equity-partner growth, while Midsize firms averaged 22.4%. The report warns that compensation-driven costs could threaten subsequent profitability.
qs: direct expenses rose a whopping 8.8%  (on a rolling 12-month change basis), while overhead expenses grew at 5.1%.
average associate compensation  rose by 11.3% per full-time equivalent (FTE) in the 12 months ending in November 2021.
Midsize firms have had strong revenue and more modest cost pressures, leading to a  22.4% average growth rate in PPEP for that sector.

kp.k: Talent competition and turnover challenged compensation-led recruitment
kp.d: An October 2021 survey of leaders at 55 U.S. firms ranked lawyer recruitment and retention, staff poaching and associate salary increases as the three leading profitability risks for 2022; talent had not featured among the previous survey's top five. Associate turnover reached 23.2% on a rolling 12-month basis through November 2021, versus 18.7% in 2019. Rates were 23.7% at Am Law 100, 22.1% at Am Law Second Hundred and 22.0% at Midsize firms. The authors question the sustainability of large compensation expenditures producing modest net headcount gains.
qs: The three highest risks to profitability all involved talent and  the intense competition reflected in the currently raging talent war.
the associate turnover rate for all firms reached 23.2%  through November 2021 on a rolling 12-month basis.
firms are spending huge amounts of money and putting their  profits at increasing risk for fairly modest returns

kp.k: Retention depends on meaning, flexibility and work-life balance
kp.d: Drawing on Herzberg's motivation framework, the authors argue that adequate pay can reduce dissatisfaction without creating satisfaction or loyalty. They emphasize recognition, meaningful work, growth and contribution. The report cites The American Lawyer's 2021 survey of 3,700 associates at 77 Am Law 200 firms: about 27% said they would leave for higher compensation, while 60% would consider leaving for better work-life balance. A separate September 2021 Thomson Reuters survey of 1,170 client-nominated Stand-Out lawyers, mostly partners, across more than 50 countries is cited for generational differences in working preferences.
qs: money alone is insufficient to create either satisfaction or loyalty.
60% of respondents said they would consider leaving their firm for a better  work-life balance.
The traditional  law firm response of just throwing more money at the problem is not likely to work as well  going forward.

kp.k: Business professionals become more important as lawyers delegate
kp.d: The report identifies retention challenges for professional staff as well as associates. It cites survey evidence that lawyers want to reduce non-billable administrative commitments not directly connected to client relationships or business development, delegating activities such as training, recruitment and knowledge management to support professionals or interested partners. This growing dependence makes loss of key business professionals especially consequential.
qs: there are also  serious retention challenges with respect to professional staff other than lawyers.
most lawyers want to reduce their commitments  to non-billable administrative activities that are not directly related to client relationships  and business development.
lawyers appear willing to delegate responsibilities to support professionals  and to those partners who might specifically wish to be involved.

kp.k: Some firms reward completed tasks rather than billed hours
kp.d: Among reported retention responses, some Midsize firms base associate compensation on tasks accomplished and work quality rather than hours billed. The report argues this can increase associates' control over their working lives, conditional on close supervision by practice or team leaders. Other responses include bonuses, accelerated promotion, recruitment of former employees, wellness support and social activities; the authors judge these measures important but likely insufficient without deeper organizational changes.
qs: providing more work flexibility by  basing associate compensation not on hours billed but rather on tasks accomplished and  quality of work.
Such an approach obviously requires close supervision by practice or team  leaders
All of these efforts are important and necessary, but they are likely not sufficient to bend  the curve on the rising turnover rate that law firms are experiencing.

kp.k: Preliminary retention findings challenge simple pay-and-hours explanations
kp.d: A preliminary Thomson Reuters analysis contrasts the lowest-turnover quarter of firms, called Stay firms, with the highest-turnover quarter, called Go firms, controlling for firm leverage. Through November 2021, annual all-attorney turnover was 8.7% versus 18.4%; average firm size was 361 versus 514 lawyers. Stay-firm lawyers billed 51 more hours annually, and Stay firms had the lowest associate compensation increases per FTE. The authors interpret these associations as suggesting retention is not primarily driven by compensation or hours, while explicitly rejecting the conclusion that lawyers prefer harder work for less pay.
qs: Through  November 2021, Stay firms recorded an annual turnover rate of 8.7%, compared to 18.4%  for Go firms.
lawyers in Stay  firms billed 51 more hours per year than their counterparts in Go firms.
These factors should not be taken as a suggestion that lawyers are happy staying at firms  that work them harder and pay them less.

kp.k: Hybrid work creates supervision, formation and fairness challenges
kp.d: The report predicts hybrid work will endure, with an emerging expectation of about three office days weekly for most lawyers. It warns that remote workers may face unequal access to assignments, mentoring, evaluation, compensation and advancement through proximity bias, with particular concerns for female lawyers. It also reports resentment where firms design flexibility for lawyers without comparable consideration for professional and support staff. The recommended response is stronger supervision, equitable training and decision procedures, and deliberate cultural connection.
qs: most firms will probably require about three days a week in the office for most lawyers.
the implementation of hybrid working arrangements presents the equity challenge of neutralizing the often unconscious bias of “out of sight, out of mind.”
modifying training programs to treat lawyers and professional staff equitably regardless  of their in-person or remote working status;

kp.k: Remote delivery supports operational redesign, not inevitable productivity decline
kp.d: The authors argue that rapid pandemic migration demonstrated firms' capacity for operational flexibility and successful remote work. A cited Thomson Reuters survey places lawyers wanting at least one remote day weekly at about 86%, double pre-pandemic levels. The report notes that productivity through November 2021 was essentially at 2019 levels and identifies potential efficiencies in office space, staffing, secretarial support, meetings and travel. It also credits tighter timekeeping, billing and collections management with improved cash collections and shorter cycles, recommending continued flexibility and transparent leadership.
qs: the number of lawyers who now want to  work remotely at least one day a week has doubled from pre-pandemic levels and is now at  about 86% of lawyers.
the pandemic has shown that remote working does not necessarily result in lower  productivity.
These efforts have resulted in noticeable upticks in cash collections and a shortening of most  firms’ billing and collection cycles.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report recommends investment in AI-assisted work processes but offers no concrete prediction about AI's effects on legal work or markets.
pts.d: The report's authors, led by James W. Jones, include AI investment among recommended actions for law firms adapting to post-pandemic operations. This is a strategic recommendation rather than a finding about AI adoption, productivity, staffing, pricing, or service quality. The wording describes assistance to work processes, not autonomous replacement of lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No AI-specific evidence is offered; the supporting context concerns technology spending generally.
pts.d: The report states that technology spending increased 7.1% during the 12 months through November 2021 and argues that the pandemic broadened acceptance of technology in legal service delivery. Its financial data come from 171 U.S.-based law firms: 51 Am Law 100 firms, 55 Am Law Second Hundred firms, and 65 midsize firms. These data do not isolate AI spending or establish any AI-specific outcome.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The recommendation belongs to the report's 2022 post-pandemic transition agenda, without an AI-specific deadline.
pts.d: AI-assisted processes are mentioned within a list of actions firms should consider as they establish new operating arrangements and align operations with their strategies. The report gives no adoption timetable, quantified forecast, or technical conditions for AI's effectiveness.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Law firms and their leaders are the intended decision-makers; specific downstream effects of AI are not identified.
pts.d: The recommendation addresses firm-level technology investment within a broader transition affecting lawyers and professional staff. The report does not specify which roles or tasks AI would change, distinguish AI effects by firm segment, or predict consequences for clients or access to justice.
